expectation: The muscle cells should build or begin the biceps in the front of the arm.

effect: The muscle cells formed the biceps; the radius still needs mineral.
reaction: The picture helped me see how the cells become muscle fibres.
reason: The front attachment is still missing bone mineral, so I’ll finish that part first.

effect: The front goal is complete: mineral strengthens the radius, and the biceps pulls it to bend the elbow.
reaction: The lever demonstration made the connection between muscle and bone clearer.
reason: The back of the arm needs a triceps, and the same muscle cells built the biceps.
expectation: The muscle cells should form the triceps in the back of the arm.

alternatives.reason: I could strengthen the back attachment first; either order works.

effect: The muscle cells formed the triceps, while the ulna still needs mineral.
reaction: The back-arm construction parallels the biceps so far.
reason: The remaining goal calls for strengthening the triceps attachment, and the ulna is awaiting mineral.
expectation: The mineral should strengthen the ulna and complete the triceps attachment.

effect: The triceps and mineralized ulna completed the back of the arm; the demonstration showed how its pull straightens the elbow.
reaction: Seeing the opposite effect of the triceps made its position matter.

mostWorthwhile.text: Finishing the front attachment was most worthwhile because the demonstration connected the biceps, tendon, radius and bending elbow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Building the back repeated the same two-part construction as the front, although it showed a different movement.

surprise.text: The same kind of muscle cells could make muscles that produce opposite movements because their attachments differ.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt especially arbitrary: the empty slots and goals explained why both muscle cells and mineral were needed.

continue.text: I would try another chapter to see more demonstrations connecting body structures to their jobs, though I hope it offers less repetition.
